title: Super trustees told to challenge insurer decisions
full_text:
Superannuation trustees have been told to independently scrutinise adverse insurance decisions after the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) found one trustee had accepted an insurer’s position without reviewing important underwriting information.
AFCA’s latest systemic issues report found the trustee had relied on an insurer’s decision to retrospectively vary or avoid insurance cover under section 29 of the Insurance Contracts Act 1984 without initially obtaining all the information supporting that decision.
The same approach had been applied to a broader group of declined claims, raising concerns about whether the trustee had adequately discharged its responsibilities to members.
“Reliance on insurer expertise does not remove the need for trustee oversight,” AFCA said.
“Trustees should consider whether they have sufficient access to the evidence supporting significant adverse insurance decisions and appropriate processes to independently consider whether further action is required for the benefit of the member.”
Following AFCA’s investigation, the trustee secured an agreement requiring the insurer to provide relevant retrospective underwriting opinions and extracts from its underwriting material.
The trustee also reviewed the affected group of declined claims, developed a more consistent approach with the insurer, established an internal working group and strengthened its policies, procedures, systems and staff training.
While the historical review did not identify grounds to change the claim outcomes, AFCA found the reforms strengthened the trustee’s ability to independently consider future adverse insurance decisions. The systemic issue was subsequently considered resolved.
Trustees were not expected to duplicate an insurer’s claims assessment, according to AFCA, but needed sufficient information to understand the basis of an adverse decision and determine whether further inquiries were required.
Member transaction failures were also identified as a systemic concern during the reporting period, including delays in investment switches and rollovers and failures to action documents submitted through digital channels.
“Receiving a valid member instruction is only the beginning of the process,” AFCA said.
“Trustees should consider whether their systems and controls can confirm that the instruction has progressed through each required stage and identify promptly where the expected transaction or account change has not occurred.”
An investigation into delayed investment switch requests identified two separate systemic issues, including a system configuration that prevented valid requests from being executed.
A separate automated process failed after money had been deducted from member accounts, preventing the intended transfers from being completed, while reconciliation controls did not detect the failed transactions promptly.
Affected members experienced actual or potential financial detriment because their instructions remained incomplete during periods of market movement.
The firm corrected the system configuration and transaction records, completed outstanding transfers and reviewed affected members for lost earnings and other financial detriments. It also paid remediation where losses were identified and strengthened transaction monitoring and reconciliation controls.
Further examination later found one member had not initially received the full remediation amount required, prompting an additional adjustment. AFCA considered the issues resolved following the corrective action, member remediation and strengthened monitoring controls.
Across financial services, systemic issues identified, investigated and resolved during the half affected 390,724 consumers and small businesses. AFCA conducted 104 detailed investigations, reported 63 systemic issues to regulators and secured $1.2 million in refunds and financial remediation.
